title: Christianity Goes Global
objective: After this level you can explain how Christianity's center of gravity shifted to Africa, Latin America and Asia, and why Pentecostal churches grew so fast.
summary: In 1910 two-thirds of Christians lived in Europe; by 2020 sub-Saharan Africa held the most. Pentecostal churches grew through lay leadership and evangelism.

cards.headline: Where does the largest share of Christians live? No longer in Europe.
cards.body: By 2020 the answer was sub-Saharan Africa. This level follows the shift, and the fast-growing churches that rode it.

cards.headline: A century-long shift
cards.body: In 1910, about two-thirds of the world's Christians lived in Europe. By 2010, only about a quarter did. By 2020, Pew found, sub-Saharan Africa had overtaken Europe as home to the most Christians: about 31% of the world's Christians, against 24% in Latin America and the Caribbean and 22% in Europe.

cards.headline: How the center moved
cards.body: Two forces did it, Pew explains. Fertility rates are much higher in Africa than in Europe, so African Christian communities grew fast. And in Western Europe, many people stopped identifying as Christian. Growth at one end, departures at the other.

cards.headline: Churches of the Spirit
cards.body: Pentecostalism takes its name from Pentecost, when, as the Acts of the Apostles describes, the Holy Spirit descended on the first Christians in Jerusalem. Pentecostals seek a later experience called baptism with the Holy Spirit, usually with speaking in tongues, and value gifts like prophecy and healing. With charismatics in other churches, they made up about 27% of the world's Christians in 2010.

cards.headline: Why they spread
cards.body: Pentecostals believe God, through the Holy Spirit, acts directly in everyday life, not just in church history. They have long treated spreading the faith as every Christian's job, not a few professionals', and they encouraged lay leadership early. That's a movement built to multiply.

cards.headline: Christianity Goes Global: the takeaways
learned: By 2020 sub-Saharan Africa held the largest share of Christians
Higher fertility and European disaffiliation drove the shift
Pentecostals grew through lay leadership and evangelism

questions.prompt: Put these regions in order of their share of the world's Christians in 2020, largest first.
questions.explanation: In 2020 about 31% of the world's Christians lived in sub-Saharan Africa, 24% in Latin America and the Caribbean, and 22% in Europe.

questions.prompt: How did sub-Saharan Africa overtake Europe in number of Christians?

options.label: Europe's Christians all moved to Africa
options.rationale: Migration isn't the cause Pew gives.

options.label: Surveys stopped counting European Christians
options.rationale: Europe is still counted, at about 22%.

options.label: Higher fertility in Africa, disaffiliation in Western Europe
A single church ordered huge new missions into sub-Saharan Africa
options.rationale: Pew points to births and departures.

questions.explanation: Much higher fertility in Africa and widespread disaffiliation in Western Europe drove the shift.

questions.prompt: Pew's world figures put a Pentecostal and a Catholic in the same group. Why?

options.label: Pentecostals are a branch of the Catholic Church
Pew counts Christians of every denomination as one group
Pew counts only people who attend Mass
options.rationale: Pew counts reported identity, not attendance.

options.label: Both groups speak in tongues
options.rationale: That's a Pentecostal practice, not the reason.

questions.explanation: Pew sorts reported religious identity into broad groups, counting all Christian denominations together.
